question.text: MR arthrography of the shoulder: do we need local anesthesia?
question.context: To assess pain intensity with and without subcutaneous local anesthesia prior to intraarticular administration of contrast medium for magnetic resonance arthrography (MRa) of the shoulder. This single-center study was conducted after an IRB waiver of authorization, between January 2010 and December 2012. All patients provided written, informed consent for the procedure. Our prospectively populated institutional database was searched, based on our inclusion criteria. There were 249 outpatients (178 men and 71 women; mean age, 44.4 years ± 14.6; range, 15-79) who underwent MRa and were enrolled in this study. Patients were excluded if they had received surgery of the shoulder before MRa, had undergone repeated MRa of the same shoulder, and/or had undergone MRa of both shoulders on the same day. Patients were randomly assigned into one of three groups. Patients in group A (n=61) received skin infiltration with local anesthesia. Patients in control group B (n=92) and group C (n=96) did not receive local anesthesia. Pain levels were immediately assessed after the injection for MRa using a horizontal visual analog scale (VAS) that ranged from 0 to 10. To compare the pain scores of the three groups for male and female patients, a two-way analysis of variance was used. A p-value equal to or less than 0.05 was considered to indicate a significant result. Patients who received local anesthesia (group A) showed a mean pain level on the VAS of 2.6 ± 2.3. In patients who did not receive local anesthetics (groups B and C), a mean pain level on the VAS of 2.6 ± 2.2 and 2.7 ± 2.4 were detected, respectively. Between the three groups, no statistically significant difference in pain intensity was detected (p=.960). There were significant differences in subjective pain perception between men and women (p=.009). Moreover, the sex difference in all three groups was equal (p=.934).

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no statistically significant difference in pain intensity between the groups receiving local anesthesia and those not receiving it. This suggests that local anesthesia is not necessary to reduce pain during MR arthrography of the shoulder.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Patients who received local anesthesia (group A) showed a mean pain level on the VAS of 2.6 ± 2.3, while those who did not receive local anesthetics (groups B and C) had mean pain levels of 2.6 ± 2.2 and 2.7 ± 2.4, respectively. No statistically significant difference in pain intensity was detected (p=.960).
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While some patients might experience discomfort, the study indicates that the pain is not significantly reduced by local anesthesia. Therefore, the need for local anesthesia is not supported by the data.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no statistically significant difference in pain intensity between patients who received local anesthesia (group A) and those who did not (groups B and C), with a p-value of 0.960. This indicates that local anesthesia did not significantly reduce pain during MR arthrography of the shoulder. The data shows that the mean pain levels were similar across all groups, suggesting that local anesthesia may not be necessary for this procedure.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The p-value of 0.960 indicating no statistically significant difference in pain intensity between groups
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: While the study focused on pain assessment, potential differential considerations include patient anxiety and comfort, but the primary outcome measure was pain intensity. The lack of significant pain reduction with local anesthesia makes the necessity of anesthesia questionable based on this evidence.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrated no statistically significant difference in pain intensity between patients who received local anesthesia (mean VAS 2.6) and those who did not (mean VAS 2.6–2.7), indicating that local anesthesia does not provide a clinically meaningful benefit. The pain perception difference between sexes was significant but consistent across groups, further supporting that anesthesia is not necessary for pain control in this context.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: No statistically significant difference in pain intensity (p=.960) between the three groups, with mean VAS scores nearly identical across groups.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Considered whether local anesthesia might be needed for patient comfort or procedural success, but the data show no benefit, so it is not indicated.

olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: No statistically significant difference in pain intensity was detected between the groups (p=.960).
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Possible concerns about local anesthesia include risk of nerve injury or allergic reaction, but the absence of significant pain difference and similar pain scores across groups suggest these risks are not outweighed by benefit in this context. Other considerations like patient preference or procedural anxiety were not evaluated in the study, but pain reduction at the injection site is not demonstrated.
